# Card 010 — NCO education to the 2026 US standard for every US NCO and every RVNAF regular and territorial NCO from 1957, each course a gate for the next promotion

*Memorandum 010 · status complete · full record: memos/010/ · generated by fie.py*

## P010a · US enlisted professional military education to the 2026 standard for every NCO of the four services from 1957: the Army's NCO Professional Development System (the 29-day Basic Leader Course, the Advanced and Senior Leader Courses, the Master Leader Course and the 10-month Sergeants Major Course) under Select, Train, Educate, Promote; the Marine Corps' Corporals Course, Sergeants School, Career and Advanced School programmes, SNCO Leadership School and First Sergeants School; the Navy and Air Force enlisted leadership continua; each course a gate for the next promotion
Every US NCO from 1957 [U]: the NCOs serving in 1957 put through the course for their grade in 1957–60 and every man promoted since through his course before promotion; about 120,000–180,000 Army and Marine course completions a year in 1957–64 and about 250,000–350,000 at the 1967–69 peak, with about as many again in the Navy and Air Force [E: D1 and D5, from NCO strengths of the period and promotion rates]; by 1 Jan 1964 every serving NCO holds the course for his grade [U: standing condition nco_education_1957] · spaces ~250–450 US personnel in RVN [E: a MACV NCO academy at about 150–250 cadre teaching the Basic Leader Course in theater to men promoted there, and NCO course cells at the field force and Marine amphibious force headquarters]; about 4,000–7,000 added instructor and staff spaces in the United States at the peak and about 2–3% of the NCO corps in school at any time, outside the ceiling [E: D2]; no troop ceiling is set (CONFIG) · arrives 1964-01-01 · FIX, SECURE, SUSTAIN · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Army 2026 courses: Basic Leader Course 29 days with 8 days in the field [M010·S2]; Advanced and Senior Leader Courses three weeks resident [M010·S4]; Master Leader Course three weeks [M010·S4]; Sergeants Major Course 10 months [M010·S4]
- Gates: STEP from 2016, each course for the next grade [M010·S1]; BLC the prerequisite for staff sergeant from 2025 [M010·S4]
- Waivers in peacetime: about 14,000 Army NCOs promoted without required education in 2015–16 [M010·S1]
- Historical: academies under AR 350-90 from 1958, 180,000 through by 1959 [M010·S6]; NCOES only from 1971 [M010·S5]; Sergeants Major Academy 1972 [H]
- NCO Candidate Course: 12 weeks plus 9 on the job, about 33,000 graduates 1967–72 [M010·S5]
- Volume: about 120,000–180,000 Army and Marine course completions a year before the war, 250,000–350,000 at the 1967–69 peak; 330,000–400,000 catch-up places in 1957–60 [E: D1]
- Cost: about 2–3% of NCOs in school at any time; 4,000–7,000 added instructors at the peak; 250–450 spaces in RVN [E: D2]
- Margin: a BLC-educated squad leader in month one about as competent as a historical one after three or four months in the field [X-010]

**Negative specification.** - **It does not make more NCOs.** The NCO shortage of 1966–69 was a shortage of men, made by the 12-month tour, the separations of senior NCOs and the build-up without reserves; the provision educates the men promoted, and its gates slow some promotions.
- **It does not keep the sergeant in the war.** The 12-month tour still takes him home; memorandum 006's unit rotation, not this, decides whether he stays with his men.
- **It does not cure the crisis of 1969–71.** Drugs, racial violence and fragging were the conscript army's crisis; an educated sergeant handles it better and is not immune to it.
- **It is not a Vietnam course.** The 2026 curricula teach large-scale combat; the war's own lessons enter only when men back from Vietnam teach it, from about 1966–67.
- **The gate will be waived.** The Army waived it about 14,000 times in peacetime; in a shortage it will be waived again, first for the junior grades.
- **It does not teach the trades.** The 2026 Advanced and Senior Leader Courses are three weeks of leadership, not technical schooling.
- **It costs sergeants.** About 2–3% of the NCO corps is in school at any time, and 4,000–7,000 senior NCOs teach instead of lead [E: D2].
- **It does not reach the Regional and Popular Forces, or the officers.** The first is outside the grant; the second is memorandum 007's.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy some of the American squad's mistakes: the patrol that is lost in the canopy and walks into a base camp, the ambush laid without security that is itself ambushed, the squad that loses its fire control in the first minute and shoots its own flank, the casualty left to bleed while the sergeant calls for help on the wrong frequency. It denies him the leaderless American platoon after its lieutenant is hit. It denies him nothing at the operational level and nothing in the sanctuary.

**Verdict.** This is a real provision for the American Army and a modest one for the war. It makes every American sergeant better at the work he was already doing, and in a war fought by squads and platoons that saves American lives and some Vietnamese ones. Its largest value falls in 1967–71, when the historical NCO corps was thinnest and youngest, because the instant sergeant now has at least the Basic Leader Course and the platoon sergeant the Advanced. It does not make more sergeants, keep them in Vietnam past their year, or touch the strategy they fight inside. Its indirect value may be the larger: every American NCO adviser has been through the courses his Vietnamese counterpart is learning, and that is what makes P010b work.

**Pushes:** US.unit_quality +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], US.casualties -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2], US.personnel_demand +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], POP.civilian_harm -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] · **Depends on:** US.unit_quality, US.political_tolerance, US.personnel_demand

## P010b · RVNAF NCO education on the 2026 US Army NCO Professional Development System for every NCO of the ARVN, Airborne, Rangers, Vietnamese Marines, VNAF and VNN and of the Regional and Popular Forces (Civil Guard and Self-Defense Corps before 1964) from 1957 (RF and PF by erratum E03): a Basic Leader Course for corporals and sergeants, an Advanced Leader Course for squad and section leaders, a Senior Leader Course for platoon sergeants, a Master Leader Course for first sergeants and battalion senior NCOs and a senior NCO course, in Vietnamese at the National NCO Academy at Nha Trang (Dong De), division and service NCO schools and the RF/PF training centres, with MAAG and MACV advisers, each course a gate for the next promotion
Every RVNAF regular and RF/PF NCO from 1957 [U]: regular NCOs about 18,000–28,000 in 1957, 35,000–50,000 in 1964 and 90,000–130,000 at the 1970 peak, RF/PF NCOs about 10,000–15,000, 25,000–40,000 and 55,000–80,000 [E: D1 and E03]; about 14,000–24,000 course completions a year in 1957–63, 27,000–45,000 in 1964–67 and 50,000–80,000 at the 1968–70 peak [E: D1 and E03, against S8's 16,522 students at the Nha Trang academy in 1970]; by 1 Jan 1964 every serving regular and territorial NCO holds the course for his grade [U: standing condition nco_education_1957] · spaces ~210–420 US personnel in RVN, of whom ~180–380 military spaces [E: an advisory detachment of 40–70 at the Nha Trang academy, teams of four to eight at 10–15 division and service NCO schools, teams of two to five at 19–37 RF/PF centres and a curriculum and translation cell at the Central Training Command; E03]; no troop ceiling is set (CONFIG) · arrives 1964-01-01 · FIX, SECURE, ADVISE, SUSTAIN · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Courses: BLC six weeks, ALC, SLC and MLC four weeks each, senior NCO course four to five months, each a gate for the next grade [U] [E: D1, the US 2026 lengths in M010·S2 and M010·S4 lengthened for translation]
- Academy: National NCO Academy, founded 1951 as the Commando School, at Nha Trang, reorganised late 1958 for leadership [M010·S8]; 16,522 students in 1970, barracks 3,320 raised to 4,520 [M010·S8]
- Historical: leader programme of seven and ten weeks only under consideration in 1964 [M010·S9]; middle NCO grades thin, promotion by seniority, across-the-board decree promotions [M010·S11]
- Commissioning drain: over 2,000 commissioned from the ranks in 1966, including 401 regular and 100 RF master sergeants first class [M010·S10]
- NCO corps: about 18,000–28,000 in 1957, 35,000–50,000 in 1964, 90,000–130,000 at the 1970 peak [E: D1]
- Throughput: 8,000–14,000 a year in 1957–63, 15,000–25,000 in 1964–67, 30,000–45,000 at the 1968–70 peak [E: D1]
- Cost: 800–1,500 Vietnamese instructors before 1964, 2,000–3,500 at the peak; 130–270 US military spaces in RVN [E: D2]
- Margin: closes about a third to a half of the gap between an average and a good ARVN company at squad and platoon level [X-010]

**Negative specification.** - **It does not reach the Regional and Popular Forces.** Their NCOs, who led the platoons that held the hamlets, keep the schooling history gave them; the territorial war's sergeants are unchanged.
- **It does not choose the officer.** An educated sergeant under a political or incompetent commander is still sent down the road into the ambush; memoranda 007 and 002 change the commander.
- **The gate can be opened by decree.** Across-the-board promotions on national occasions were historical; a gate the government can override is a standard, not a law.
- **It costs the best sergeants.** About 800–1,500 Vietnamese instructors before 1964 and 2,000–3,500 at the peak, on top of memorandum 009's 2,000–3,000 drill sergeants.
- **It does not cure desertion.** Pay, family and posting drive it; the course touches the leader who counsels the soldier, not the pay that feeds his family.
- **It does not stop the commissioning drain.** The best senior NCOs are the best candidates for commission, and over 2,000 were commissioned in 1966 alone.
- **It teaches the technique of the after-action review, not the culture of telling the truth.** The course can teach a sergeant to report failure; it cannot make his officers want to hear it.
- **It does not reach above the company.** The battles the ARVN lost above the NCO are lost the same way.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the ARVN platoon that sleeps in its night position without listening posts, the squad that fires all its ammunition in the first minutes and then runs, the company that loses its fire control when its officer is hit, and the patrol that takes the same path every evening. It denies him some of the ARVN's tactical predictability below the company commander, and some of the looting and abuse in the hamlets that a sergeant who controls his men prevents. It does not deny him the decision above the company.

**Verdict.** This is a substantial provision for the ARVN, larger than P010a is for the Americans, because the ARVN's NCO corps was its thinnest layer and nobody before this grant had built it. With memorandum 009's trained private and memorandum 007's educated lieutenant, the regular army from 1964 has, for the first time, a trained leader at every level from the squad to the company. That changes how ARVN small units fight at night, how they keep their weapons and trucks running, and how they treat the people in the hamlets they pass through. Its costs are the best sergeants taken to teach, in the year the army can least spare them, and a gate the government can open whenever it wishes. It does not reach the territorial forces, the commanders above the company, or the pay that keeps the soldier's family fed. A better sergeant under a bad colonel is still under a bad colonel; but in a war of squads and platoons, a better sergeant is most of what the soldier sees of the army.

**Pushes:** ARVN.effectiveness +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], ARVN.self_sufficiency +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], ARVN.desertion -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2], RFPF.effectiveness +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], US.personnel_demand +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] · **Depends on:** ARVN.leadership, ADVISE.leverage, GVN.corruption, ECON.inflation, ARVN.desertion, ENEMY.engagement_control, POP.night_control, GVN.admin_capacity, STRIKE.responsiveness, ARVN.self_sufficiency

- P015b (memo 015) pushes +2 to +6 [% of the RVNAF's fire support delivered by its own guns and aircraft] by the end of P4 (low) on ARVN.self_sufficiency.fire_support — 2–6 points more of the RVNAF's fire support delivered by its own aircraft by 1971: about 400–800 VNAF gunship sorties a month, each worth several hours of night fire, in place of US gunship and tactical air at night
- P015b (memo 015) pushes +3 to +8 [% of the RVNAF's fire support delivered by its own guns and aircraft] by the end of P6 (low) on ARVN.self_sufficiency.fire_support — 3–8 points more of the RVNAF's fire support its own by the end of 1974, if the U is flown and maintained after the Americans leave; bounded by the SA-7 and radar AAA that historically drove VNAF aircraft above useful altitudes

### VCI.strength
- P002a (memo 002) pushes -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] — Village cadre identified and arrested on evidence, legal cadre forced underground; slow, cumulative and confined to villages the state holds
- P006a (memo 006) pushes -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] — Cadres above the hamlet named, arrested and tried from 1965 rather than 1968, where night security exists

## Settled positions on these variables

- **POSTNA-2** · vars: POP.night_control, RFPF.effectiveness · Night control of a hamlet is held only by security resident in it with a means of calling help and a reaction that arrives in the dark; mobile forces that leave at dusk do not change it (TNA G-2)
- **POSTNA-5** · vars: US.political_tolerance, US.credibility_gap, US.casualties · The American political clock is spent by casualties, cost and time, and fastest by the discovery that reported progress was false; a provision that improves a metric without improving the war shortens the clock (TNA G-5, G-10)
- **POS001-1** · vars: POP.land_tenure, POP.gvn_legitimacy, POP.night_control · Land reform changes what the government's arrival means, not whether it arrives: its value in any hamlet equals the night security behind it, and titles issued are never evidence of allegiance (001 §2 F001-4, F001-10; §4.P2)
- **POS001-4** · vars: POP.gvn_legitimacy, VCI.strength · A one-band gain in the countryside's allegiance does not carry into the conventional battles of 1972 and 1975; the end state turns on the military balance after the American withdrawal, and political gains are necessary but not sufficient to move it (001 §4.N)
- **POS002-1** · vars: GVN.police, FIND.vci, POP.night_control · A rural police and Special Branch attack the infrastructure, not the main force; their value in any village equals the night security beside them, and where they work best their arrest count falls, so arrest counts and quotas are never the measure of them (002 F002-11, F002-17; §4.P2)
- **POS002-3** · vars: GVN.police, GVN.political_stability, POP.gvn_legitimacy · A stronger and better-recorded police in a coup-prone state is used by the government of the day against its domestic opposition, and its records are a list of loyalties the enemy can capture; both costs are paid and do not outweigh the gain in the held belt (002 F002-9, F002-16; §4.P2, §4.P3)
- **POS004-1** · vars: RFPF.effectiveness, POP.night_control, ENEMY.engagement_control · Infantry small arms change how the fights the enemy accepts go, never which fights he accepts; at the outpost their value equals the platoon's presence after dark and the reaction behind it, and the enemy's answer to a better-armed post is to attack what is not rearmed (004 F004-1, F004-3, F004-16; §4.P1)
- **POS004-2** · vars: ARVN.effectiveness, US.unit_quality, US.political_tolerance · In this war the ARVN and the RF/PF carry modern carbines from 1964, and the 1967 M16 crisis and inquiry and the 1968–69 rearmament do not occur; from 1969 the historical army has caught up, and the remaining difference is the squad gun, the marksman and the practice (004 F004-6; §4.P2–P4)
- **POS004-3** · vars: ARVN.self_sufficiency, LOG.distribution · Abundant American ammunition from 1964 deepens the RVNAF's dependence on volume of fire; the 1974 ration falls hardest on the squad gun, and the divisional hoards built against it are lost in the collapse of March 1975 (004 F004-15; §4.P6)
- **POS005-2** · vars: ARVN.self_sufficiency, FIX.capability, US.political_tolerance · In this war the defence of besieged positions from 1965 rests on the B-52J and an American coordinate cell; it is far stronger while American air power is present and leaves the RVNAF more dependent on it when it goes (005 §2 F005-20)
- **POSCP01-2** · vars: ADVISE.leverage, ARVN.self_sufficiency · In this war the American lever was used to protect the Republic's honest institutions from its own governments and never to make the Republic own the instruments of the conventional war (coordinates, reconnaissance, guided weapons, ammunition stocks); the dependence deepened by memoranda 004 and 005 was never contested by the instrument that could have contested it (CP01 §3)
- **POS006-1** · vars: FIND.vci, VCI.strength, POP.night_control · Phung Hoang adds the layer above the hamlet to what the Special Branch knows, only where the night is held; outside the held belt it is the historical Phoenix whatever its rules, and its audited count, which falls where it works best, is the measure, never its arrest count (006 F006-15, F006-18, F006-26)
- **POS006-2** · vars: US.unit_quality, US.casualties, ENEMY.engagement_control · Unit rotation makes the American battalion fight better in the contacts it gets and changes neither which contacts it gets nor the late-war breakdown of discipline; it gives the enemy a relief window to aim at, and it does not prevent atrocity (006 F006-6, F006-16, F006-19)
- **POS006-3** · vars: ADVISE.leverage, ARVN.self_sufficiency · The selected advisory corps deepens influence, not authority; its durable values are continuity across the American unit's relief and honest reporting, and a better adviser deepens the advised unit's dependence on American fire unless he hands over the radio, which works for artillery, the VNAF and medevac and not for the B-52J (006 F006-2, F006-17, F006-23)
- **POS006-4** · vars: FIND.vci, INTEL.penetration, GVN.political_stability · In this war the national Phung Hoang file, built to warrant standard from 1964, was moved into the Central Intelligence Organization in 1970, consolidated in one building for the 1971 election, and captured intact on 30 April 1975 with the I Corps files a month earlier; the accuracy that made it valuable to the Republic made it more valuable to the victors (006 §4.P4, §4.P6; EV002-6, EV000-94, EV000-98)
- **POS006-5** · vars: FIND.vci, US.credibility_gap · In this war there was no ICEX, no Phoenix quota and no 1969 discovery of false claims; the attack on the infrastructure had an audited count from 1965, and "Phoenix" became a press scandal in March 1967 over the Duc Thanh raid rather than in 1970 over the programme (006 §4.P2, §4.P3; EV006-4, EV000-54)
- **POS006-6** · vars: US.unit_quality, US.casualties, US.personnel_demand · In this war American battalions deploy, are relieved and withdraw as units; the estimated saving of 1,000–2,000 American lives in 1966–69 is a judgment on a rate of 3–6 percent shown so far only at Dien Ban, and does not move the casualty band (006 §4.P2, §4.H; EV006-3)
- **POS007-1** · vars: ARVN.leadership, ARVN.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · In this war the ARVN's battalions from 1965–67 are commanded by officers a board chose on written criteria and two raters' reports, for eighteen months, with relief for cause; this puts ARVN effectiveness at the cap of the bands in 1966–68, and the enemy answers by declining the better battalion and attacking the unreformed unit beside it, so the gain appears as battalions not lost rather than in any metric (007 §4.P2; EV007-2, EV007-3)
- **POS007-3** · vars: GVN.political_stability, ARVN.leadership, INTEL.penetration · An educated field-grade officer corps whose promotion is blocked at the top becomes a faction in the palace's eyes; in this war the colonels' petition of September 1970 was answered by moving about forty regimental and battalion commanders out of the field before Lam Son 719, and COSVN targeted the passed-over officers from 1968 with small yield (007 §4.P3, §4.P4; EV007-5, EV000-52)
- **POS007-4** · vars: US.unit_quality, US.casualties, POP.civilian_harm · American officer education from 1957 improves platoon and company leadership and saves American lives at a rate of perhaps one to three percent of small-unit deaths in 1965–69, below a band; it does not prevent My Lai or the late-war decay of discipline, which came from the command climate above the lieutenant (007 §4.P2, §4.P3; EV000-23)
- **POSMT01-1** · vars: ARVN.self_sufficiency, VNAF.capability, ADVISE.leverage, ARVN.leadership · Rung (a) is reaffirmed after seven memoranda on its mechanism, not its date: every provision so far is American-owned and withdrawn by 1973, or works below the level of command at which 1972 and 1975 were decided, or was captured by the palace when the American lever lapsed in 1970–71; the rung will not move until a provision reaches an air arm the Republic owns, sustainment that survives the 1974 appropriation, or the choice of the corps commanders (MT01 M-12)
- **POSMT01-3** · vars: HANOI.will, PAVN.strength_south, ARVN.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · The date of the Republic's fall, 30 April 1975 within a window of about 27 April to the first days of May, is derived and not carried: it was set by Hanoi's resolution of 25 March to finish before the rains and by the 1st Corps' march, and only a delay of about three weeks or more in the collapse of I and II Corps would have moved it, by putting the assault into the rains; better ARVN units act on fights the PAVN bypasses and do not reach that threshold (MT01 M-12; EVMT01-4, EV000-96)
- **POSMT01-4** · vars: POP.night_control, VCI.strength, POP.gvn_legitimacy, FIND.vci · The countryside at the end of 1972 is not history's: where a PAVN division sat in the peopled lowlands (northern Binh Dinh, Quang Tri) the gains of 1964–71 were lost, while the held belt of the Delta and the Saigon region kept its posts and files and stays one band better at night and against the infrastructure; the government's legitimacy returns to history's through the decrees of 1972 (MT01 M-4; EVMT01-1, EVMT01-2, EVMT01-3)
- **POSMT01-5** · vars: US.political_tolerance, US.casualties, US.credibility_gap · The sum of the American lives the provisions saved is a judgment of about 2,500–5,000, mostly in 1965–69, five to nine percent of the historical dead, below a band; it does not move tolerance, and the changes in the record that bear on the 1974 appropriation roughly cancel, so the vote stands as history's until a provision changes what the Republic needs Congress to pay for (MT01 M-7; EV000-89)
- **POSMT01-6** · vars: ARVN.desertion, ARVN.effectiveness, POP.displacement · The ARVN's corps dissolved in March 1975 because the soldiers' families lived beside their units in the path of the offensive and the men went to them; no reform of the officer corps or the battalions reaches this, and it absorbed the gains of memoranda 004, 006 and 007 in the last campaign (MT01 open search; EV000-94, EV000-95)
- **POS008-1** · vars: ARVN.self_sufficiency, ADVISE.leverage, US.political_tolerance · A domestic arsenal, battery works and rebuild depot stretch the aid dollar in 1974–75 only if the RVNAF has been made to buy from them while American supply was free; this headquarters adopts a domestic share enforced by the Aid Compliance Board from 1965, and the stretch changes what the fiscal 1975 appropriation buys, not the vote (008 §2 F008-2, F008-20, F008-23)
- **POS008-2** · vars: POP.night_control, RFPF.effectiveness, STRIKE.responsiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · A radio kept on the air at the post supplies the means of calling help in POSTNA-2 and moves the post's binding constraint to the reaction and fire within range; the Front answers by attacking the relief and the posts that cannot call, and the radio's gain appears as attacks not made (008 §2 F008-1, F008-3, F008-6, F008-16)
- **POS008-3** · vars: ARVN.self_sufficiency, US.political_tolerance, HANOI.will · In this war the Republic's own arsenal and battery works stretched the fiscal 1975 appropriation to about $850 million–$1 billion of history's and kept its ammunition and communications from going dark in 1974, but delayed the collapse of I and II Corps by days, not the three weeks that would have moved the date; domestic sustainment without an air arm the Republic owns and a choice of corps commanders does not move the rung (008 §4.P6, §4.N; EV000-89, EVMT01-4)
- **POS008-4** · vars: RFPF.effectiveness, POP.night_control, STRIKE.responsiveness · From 1967 the territorial post's first call is for fire, not men, after the Front's ambush of the relief at My Phuoc Tay; this makes the post cheaper to hold and keeps the platoon behind its wire, so that the post is held better and the hamlet outside it is not, and the call passes to Vietnamese district guns in 1970–71 (008 §4.P2, §4.P4; EV008-4, EV008-7)
- **POS008-5** · vars: GVN.corruption, ADVISE.leverage, ARVN.self_sufficiency · The Directorate of Defence Industry fell to the palace in February 1970 with the four other institutions built behind the American lever; its output and the domestic share survived because the Joint General Staff wanted them, and honest lot acceptance did not, costing perhaps a tenth to a fifth of the base's 1974 value (008 §4.P4; EV002-6)
- **POS009-1** · vars: ARVN.effectiveness, RFPF.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · Basic training changes how the fights the enemy accepts go and how many wounded live after them, never which fights he accepts; in this war the ARVN of 1964–65 stands a band above history on the course, the carbine and the educated lieutenant together, and the enemy answers the trained soldier with the mine, the sapper and the untrained target (009 §4.P1, §4.P2; EV002-2, EV009-2, EV009-4)
- **POS009-2** · vars: MED.survival, US.casualties, US.political_tolerance · In this war every soldier of both armies is taught the tourniquet in basic training; the saving is a judgment on a rate of two to four percent of killed in action, shown at Albany and in the first wave of Tet, about 900–1,900 Americans and 4,000–12,000 South Vietnamese, below a band on every variable and proof against enemy adaptation (009 §4.P2, §4.P3, §4.N; EV000-23, EV000-42)
- **POS009-3** · vars: ARVN.desertion, ECON.inflation, VCI.strength · Training does not reach desertion, which follows the soldier's pay, rice and family; the trained deserter carries the course home, and a few hundred a year in the Saigon belt carry it to the Front's guerrillas (009 §4.P2; EV009-3)
- **POS010-1** · vars: ARVN.effectiveness, RFPF.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · In this war every RVNAF and territorial NCO since 1957 has passed the course for his grade, and empty squads are given to corporals first class who passed the leader's course; this changes how squads and posts fight the fights the enemy accepts, never which fights he accepts, and the enemy answers by passing the units that keep the routine and attacking those that do not, so the gain appears as companies not destroyed and posts not attacked (010 F010-19, F010-25; EV010-3, EV010-4)
- **POS010-3** · vars: US.unit_quality, US.casualties, US.personnel_demand · American NCO education from 1957 makes the American squad better in the patrol base and the night ambush and saves about 300–900 American lives, a judgment on a rate of one to three percent of small-unit deaths, below a band; it costs the senior NCOs of 1966–67 and does not prevent the decay of 1969–71 (010 F010-12, F010-18, F010-22; EV010-2, EV010-5)
- **POS010-4** · vars: ARVN.self_sufficiency, STRIKE.responsiveness · The American NCO course carries the habit of fixing the enemy and calling fire down to the ARVN squad; it is a strength the Republic owns only where the gun at the other end is Vietnamese, as at Long My, and a dependence everywhere else (010 F010-24; EV008-7)
- **POSCP02-1** · vars: ARVN.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · In this war the ARVN battalion of 1966–68 stands at the cap of the bands through four memoranda (007, 009, 010 and 004 before them), and the battalions broken in 1966–67 are about two-fifths to a half fewer than history's, a judgment whose factors overlap and whose upper bound is the "about half" of 010; any further provision on the battalion is measured in that running sum and not in the band, and none of it changes which fights the enemy accepts (CP02 §3, §5)
- **POSCP02-2** · vars: ENEMY.engagement_control, POP.civilian_harm, VCI.strength · Every provision since 004 that improved the RVNAF below the company was answered by the enemy moving his war to what the provision did not reach: the relief, the borrowed district, the mine in the hamlet, the untrained self-defence group; the provisions' gain in the army is paid for in part by the unprotected population, and every later provision touching the army or the posts names the target the enemy moves to and estimates the cost there (CP02 §1, §6; EV008-4, EV009-2, EV009-4, EV010-4)
- **REVR01-1** · reverses POSCP02-1 · vars: ARVN.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · The judgment of POSCP02-1 on the war stands: the ARVN battalions broken in 1966–67 are about two-fifths to a half fewer than history's, a judgment whose factors overlap and whose upper bound is the "about half" of 010, and none of it changes which fights the enemy accepts. What is reversed is its method: further provisions on the ARVN battalion are no longer measured outside the variable because the variable is capped. They are measured on the v1.0.6 scale, in the range of ARVN effectiveness and the facet they act on, and the running sum feeds that range (R01)
- **POS011-2** · vars: US.political_tolerance, ARVN.self_sufficiency · American military aid to the RVNAF is about $950 million for fiscal 1975, buying through the domestic stretch about what $1.2 billion bought historically, with supplementals of about $150 million in March and $175 million in May 1975 and about $800 million for fiscal 1976; the money reached fuel, aircraft and heavy rounds and saved perhaps 1,500–4,000 of the Republic's dead in 1974, and it never reached the soldier's pay or the artillery duel with the 130mm (011 F011-2, F011-21; EV000-89, EV000-91, EV011-2, EV000-97, EV011-3)
- **POS011-3** · vars: GVN.political_stability, ARVN.effectiveness, ARVN.desertion · Thieu refused the Dalat study on 11 March 1975 and gave no withdrawal order on 13–14 March, because he held the money and the President's message; the refusal cost half the Highland force and the 2nd Division and delayed the collapse of I and II Corps by three to five weeks, and in May he took the study's method for SOUTHERN WALL; the counter-directional finding is the mechanism of the gain (011 F011-20; EV000-94, EV000-95, EV011-3)
- **POS011-4** · vars: POP.civilian_harm, US.credibility_gap, US.unit_quality · The Son My massacre is removed by stipulation and isolated: there is no Peers inquiry, no Calley trial and no inquiry into the Americal Division's command climate, every other killing of civilians in Quang Ngai stands, and Son My's people live under the Front; the public's verdict on the war is unchanged because it was in before November 1969 (011 F011-5, F011-10, F011-11; EV000-46, EV000-63, EV000-72)
- **POS011-5** · vars: US.unit_quality, US.political_tolerance, US.casualties · A quarter of the historically inducted enlisted voluntarily in the same jobs (Reading A); draft calls are a quarter smaller and the force is unchanged; the volunteers die at the draftees' rate and are about half as likely to be on the drug and refusal lists of 1970–71, with no change to any battle (011 F011-15, F011-19; EV010-5)
- **REV011-1** · reverses POSMT01-3 · vars: HANOI.will, PAVN.strength_south, ARVN.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · The method of POSMT01-3 stands: the date of the fall is derived from Hanoi's calendar, and only a delay of about three weeks or more in the collapse of I and II Corps moves it. What is reversed is the date. In this war the collapse came three to five weeks late, because Thieu gave no withdrawal order on 13–14 March 1975; the Politburo put the assault on Saigon back to the dry season of 1975–76, and the fall is expected between February and May 1976 (011; EVMT01-4, EV000-94, EV000-95)
- **REV011-2** · reverses POSMT01-5 · vars: US.political_tolerance, US.casualties, US.credibility_gap · The sum of the American lives saved stands at about 3,700–7,800 and does not move tolerance. What is reversed is the vote: the fiscal 1975 appropriation is no longer history's, because the President who fought for it was not fighting impeachment, and the April 1975 request is Nixon's and partly voted (011 F011-17; EV000-89, EV000-97)
- **POS012-1** · vars: VCI.strength, FIND.vci, POP.night_control · In this war a combined interagency task force with lift, raid teams and cross-province warrants from 1964 broke the Front's district government of the held belt from its edge in 1965–67, about a third to a half of the district layer in 12–18 provinces beyond what the police and the district centres had done; it reached committees beyond the held belt only as far as helicopter and warrant, never into the base areas, and its gains hold only where the posts hold the night (012 F012-27; EV012-4)
- **POS012-3** · vars: INTL.allied_forces, POP.civilian_harm · In this war the Korean forces accepted combined operational control only with a countersignature and a national referral, which put Korean soldiers beyond the Republic's law; the Korean element of the task force was withdrawn after Hoa Thanh in April 1966 and Korean soldiers took no further part in targeting the infrastructure (012 EV012-3, EV012-5)
- **POSCP03-2** · vars: FIND.vci, ENEMY.engagement_control · A picture of the enemy's political organisation warns of where his political apparatus will act and not of when or in what strength his main forces will; at Tet 1968 the files held the caches, committees and guides of the uprising, the combined estimate read them as local, and MACV's judgment of the main effort and the Joint General Staff's leave order absorbed the warning, so the surprise was national and the change was confined to the corps centres of III and IV Corps (EV000-42, EV012-8; the user's question of 25 Nov 2026)
- **POSCP03-3** · vars: POP.night_control, VCI.strength, FIND.vci · Night control judged by corps in units for the first time: the land, the police, the posts and the task force hold about 8–14 points more of III Corps' and 6–12 points more of IV Corps' rural people after dark than history's by the end of 1967, about six months to a year ahead of history's pacification there, and about 3–9 points more at the end of 1974; I and II Corps never move more than a few points, and those two corps decided 1972 and 1975 (CP03 §8; the user's question of 25 Nov 2026)
- **POS014-1** · vars: FIND.vci, VCI.strength, SANCT.cambodia · In this war a night raid force on the Front's senior apparatus from 1964 drove that apparatus out of the provinces it administered and across the Cambodian border by 1967, where no allied instrument could reach it; the raid force's falling yield from 1967 measures that success and not its failure, and the displacement is never reported as a reduction in the Front's organisation (014 §4.P2, F014-19, F014-21; EV014-5, EV014-7)
- **POS014-4** · vars: US.personnel_demand, ARVN.effectiveness · In this war a unit committed whole to one theater for eleven years held its headcount and spent its experience: about a quarter of its operators by the end of 1967 were selected after the war began, and its sustained rate was about half what its first months implied (014 §4.P2, F014-13; EV014-1, EV014-3)
- **POS015-1** · vars: RFPF.effectiveness, POP.night_control, STRIKE.responsiveness · In this war a gunship is over a post under attack within 15–30 minutes on a clear night in the net from January 1964; this supplies the reaction that arrives in the dark of POSTNA-2 for the post, not the hamlet, and the Front answers by attacking in cloud, beyond the net, from inside the hamlet and by day (015 F015-1, F015-5, F015-12)
- **POS015-2** · vars: VNAF.capability, ARVN.self_sufficiency, ADVISE.leverage · The VNAF's AC-130U wing, at strength from the end of 1969, is the first instrument of the air war the Republic owns and keeps after 1973; it works at the level of the territorial war and not of the command decisions of 1972 and 1975, and it flies on the appropriation (015 F015-4, F015-19)
- **POS015-3** · vars: RFPF.effectiveness, POP.night_control, STRIKE.responsiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · In this war from 1964 the Front does not assault a covered post on a clear night within the gunship net, and it moves its night attacks to the monsoon cloud, to the posts beyond the net and into the hamlets; on the coast of I and II Corps the monsoon nights are the Front's until the VNAF's radar gunships cover them from 1969 (015 EV015-1, EV015-2, EV015-4)
- **POS015-4** · vars: VNAF.capability, ARVN.self_sufficiency, POP.night_control · The VNAF's gunship wing holds the Delta's posts at night in 1973–75 and cannot fly over the PAVN's divisions, which bring their own air defence; it changes which posts the Republic holds and not which divisions it can stop, and it does not move the critical path of 1975 (015 EV015-8, EV000-91, EV000-95)
- **REVCP04-1** · reverses POS004-3 · vars: ARVN.self_sufficiency, LOG.distribution · The first half of POS004-3 stands: abundant American ammunition from 1964 deepened the RVNAF's dependence on volume of fire, and the 1974 ration fell hardest on the squad gun. What is reversed is the hoards' fate, because this war has no collapse of March 1975: the Hue hoard of about 3 million rounds was destroyed in place on 17 April (EV000-94), the hoards of I and II Corps were not abandoned in March and what the Highlands and Quang Ngai held went with them in April, the 18th Division held Xuan Loc through the rains on more ammunition than history's April could find (EV000-96), and the stocks of III and IV Corps remain the Republic's at the end of 1975 (CP04 §8; small-arms study Q-3)
- **POSCP04-1** · vars: US.casualties, US.political_tolerance · The running sum of American lives saved by the provisions is about 4,100–9,500, a judgment on the record's rates: REV011-2's 3,700–7,800 as memorandum 012 moved it to about 3,750–8,100, less memorandum 014's 60–180 American dead and plus memorandum 015's 500–1,500 at the Ia Drang and over the posts; it is about 7–16 percent of the war's American dead and does not move tolerance, and memoranda 014 and 015, which began from POSMT01-5's superseded 2,500–5,000, are read on this figure (CP04 §8)
- **POSCP04-2** · vars: SUBVERT.defection, FIND.vci · In this war the raid force and the targeted offer to rally worked from the same file and the same names and worked against each other at the province level: from 1966 a province or region cadre who expected a raid moved to Memot and later Kratie rather than rallying, so the raids lowered defection among the senior cadre of the Saigon belt and the upper Delta; the offer kept its value for district and village cadres, who had nowhere to go (CP04 Part 1 §3; EV014-5)

- **P002a** · National Police Reform Programme, 1964: a resident rural constabulary with a police post in every village, a rebuilt Police Special Branch with sole charge of intelligence on the VC infrastructure, a Police Field Force raised two years early, a national identity and family census, a police pay and career statute, and judicial safeguards on arrest and detention · One national programme: the National Police grown from about 19,000–22,000 in January 1964 to about 70,000 by the end of 1966 and about 95,000 by the end of 1968, of whom about 24,000 rural police resident in villages and about 7,500 Special Branch [E: village and district counts of the period, the historical growth to 88,000 by 1970, and training throughput] · spaces ~520 US personnel, of whom ~150 military spaces [E: about 300 USAID Public Safety advisers against the historical 144 of December 1965, about 150 Army military police and CID training-team spaces, about 70 contractor technicians for the identity system]; about 40 British, Malaysian and Australian police advisers outside US spaces · SECURE, FIND, SUBVERT · arrives 1964-01-01 · active · memo 002
- **P002b** · Provincial Administration Reform, 1964: merit-based selection of province and district chiefs by an independent Provincial Administration Selection Board, by competitive examination, assessment and vetting, with appointment from a ranked list, a guaranteed two-year tenure removable only for cause, an independent Inspectorate of Provincial Administration, a pay and allowance reform, and a mandatory course before posting · About 290 chief posts (44–45 province chiefs and 239–243 district chiefs) and about 330 deputy posts, filled by competition over 1964–65 [E: the province and district counts of the period, one deputy for administration in each province and district] · spaces ~90 US personnel, of whom ~30 military spaces [E: a small advisory staff to the Selection Board and the Inspectorate, assessment-centre specialists, and province senior advisers' share of the inspection work] · SECURE, ADVISE · arrives 1964-01-01 · active · memo 002

- **P004a** · M4A1 carbine with the Upper Receiver Group – Improved (URG-I: Geissele Automatics upper, Daniel Defense 14.5-inch 1:7 barrel, mid-length gas, Mk16 13.5-inch M-LOK rail, SureFire SF4P flash hider) and Aimpoint CompM5 2 MOA red-dot sight, firing M855A1 5.56mm, 2026 configuration · All rifles and carbines of US forces and the RVNAF, and all RF/PF [U]: a first increment of about 600,000 carbines and sights in 1964, rising to about 1.7–1.9 million cumulative by 1972 [E: RVNAF 514,000 in 1964 and about 1,048,000 in 1971–72 per S9, US strength rising to about 540,000 at peak, plus a 10% float] · spaces ~250 [E: about 120 new-equipment training spaces in the first year, about 80 small-arms and optics repair technicians at the depots, and about 50 added small-arms advisers to the RF/PF training centres; no troop ceiling is set, but each space still costs] · SECURE, FIX, ADVISE, SUSTAIN · arrives 1964-01-01 · active · memo 004
- **P004b** · Knight's Armament Company M110A2 7.62mm semi-automatic rifle (20-inch free-floated match barrel, integral suppressor, 12-inch M-LOK handguard, collapsible stock) with SIG Sauer TANGO6T 1-6x24mm first-focal-plane illuminated variable-power scope, firing M118LR and M80A1 7.62mm, issued one per infantry squad as the designated marksman's rifle, 2026 configuration · One per US and ARVN infantry squad [U]: about 5,000 rifles and scopes in 1964, about 13,000 cumulative by 1972 [E: about 120 ARVN, Ranger, Airborne and Marine battalions of about 36 squads in 1964 rising to about 180 by 1972, plus up to about 112 US Army and Marine manoeuvre battalions at the 1968–69 peak, plus a 10% float] · spaces ~120 [E: marksman instructor teams of about 60 at the training centres and about 60 match-rifle and scope armourers; the marksmen themselves are squad members already counted] · FIX, SECURE, STRIKE · arrives 1964-01-01 · active · memo 004

## Gap register (latest status)

- **G-1** · A state without a foundation · narrowed · Land, police, merit chiefs and the Commission give the Republic a government in the held belt from 1964; it is captured by the palace when the American lever lapses in 1970–71, and its foundation in the countryside does not carry into the conventional war (CP01)
- **G-2** · Who holds the countryside after dark · narrowed · III and IV Corps hold about 8–14 and 6–12 points more of their rural people after dark than history's by 1967 and about 3–9 points more at the end of 1974 (POSCP03-3); from 1964 a gunship answers a post inside the net within 15–30 minutes on a clear night, and from 1969 the VNAF's radar gunships answer about two-thirds of the posts through cloud (POS015-1, POS015-3); the Front moved to the cloud, the hamlet's edge and the posts beyond the net, and I and II Corps never moved more than a few points
- **G-3** · Identifying the infrastructure inside the population · narrowed · The national file holds the enemy's political organisation to the end of 1975 and warns of where, not when (POSCP03-2); the raid force drove the senior apparatus it names across the Cambodian border by 1967, so the file names men nobody can reach (POS014-1)
- **G-4** · The officer corps: selection, leadership, desertion, corruption · narrowed · Below the regiment the RVNAF is led by board-chosen, educated officers and schooled NCOs from 1965–66, two-fifths to a half fewer battalions are broken in 1966–67, and the enemy declines them; the divisions and corps stay the palace's choices, and the decisive commands of 1972 and 1975 are chosen as historically (CP02)
- **G-5** · The American political clock · open · The provisions saved about 4,100–9,500 American lives on the record's rates (POSCP04-1), about 7–16 percent of the war's dead; tolerance is unmoved in every phase, and the fiscal 1975 appropriation is larger than history's only because there was no Watergate (POS011-1)
- **G-6** · Advisory leverage and its limits · open · The Aid Compliance Board is a real lever until 1969 and lapses with the withdrawal; it was used for governance and never for the RVNAF's self-sufficiency (CP01)
- **G-7** · Finding and fixing the main force · open · The enemy is easier to see in the open and exactly as hard to find under canopy; he still chooses every fight except the siege (CP01)
- **G-8** · Sanctuary and the theory of attrition · open · Cambodia is counted from 1965 and its caches fall in ten days in 1970; from 1967 it also holds the Front's provincial government of the upper Delta and the Saigon belt, driven there by the raids (C014-2), and the sanctuaries still regenerate the main force in every phase
- **G-9** · The Trail: throughput required against capacity · open · The opening strike on the North gave the Trail a second cause of its larger capacity: the trucks Moscow sent in place of heavy plant (C013-1); bombing still taxes arrivals by about a tenth at best, and the South's needs are a few tens of tons a day (POSTNA-4)
- **G-10** · The measurement problem · narrowed · R03 put every variable in a natural unit and entered 45 of history's figures; about 60 headline anchors remain unresearched, among them refugees, legitimacy, VCI strength and enemy initiative at the end of 1971, which CP04 judged as differences from history without history's figure, and the ledger of the Republic's small arms after 1966 (small-arms study Q-4)
- **G-11** · The sea and Sihanoukville · narrowed · The sea route closed in 1964; Sihanoukville opened eighteen months early and was counted, not stopped, until Lon Nol closed it in 1970 (CP01)
- **G-12** · Air power against a dispersed, night-moving enemy · narrowed · Decisive against the fixed and the measured, nothing against a society that has stopped owning anything worth a guided bomb (POSCP03-1); at night over a post the gunships of memorandum 015 hold the clear nights, and the Vietnamese radar gunships the cloudy ones, but no gunship flies over a PAVN division with its own air defence (POS015-4)
- **G-13** · No single manager of the war · open · CORDS on its historical date and form; the provisions created no single manager, only better inheritances for it (CP01)
- **G-14** · No lever on Hanoi's will · open · The heaviest opening blow the record holds moved Hanoi's will not at all (rung 4 throughout, R03) and its timing only through a Republic that did not collapse (EVMT01-4)
- **G-15** · The theater base · open · Unchanged by any provision; the rearmament's ammunition and the J's kits ride the historical base (CP01)
- **G-16** · Personnel spaces · narrowed · Unit rotation, a selected eighteen-month advisory corps, drill sergeants and NCO schools draw on one pool of American senior NCOs, bringing the 1967 shortage forward three to six months and deepening it; spaces remain trivial against a ceiling of none, and nothing a provision has built survives the withdrawal of 1973 (CP02)
- **G-17** · The soldier's family · open · The devaluation of June 1966 cut the private's rice by a third and his trained desertion carried the course to the Front around Saigon; no provision has touched pay against inflation, dependants' housing or the movement of families, and in March 1975 the corps dissolved toward them (CP02)
- **G-18** · Civilian harm has no holder · open · POP.civilian_harm is pushed by more than a dozen provisions and judged nowhere outside one study value; from 1964 the merit list's district chiefs clear fire within 300 metres of a post and become the arbiters of harm beside the hamlets at night (C015-1), and from 1970 those chiefs are the palace's choices; the record does not say whether harm rose after 1970, and a study or checkpoint must judge it by phase (air-war study Q-6)
- **G-19** · The war in northern Laos and on the rivers · open · The record holds no account of Barrel Roll and the Plain of Jars after 1964, nor of the riverine and coastal war after 1965 (Game Warden, the Vietnamese Navy's river groups, Market Time's later years); each shapes the Trail, the Delta and the sea route the provisions touched (air-war Q-4, maritime Q-3, Q-4)
- **G-20** · The Republic's imported technology after 1973 · open · The record traces the gunship wing's fuel in the ration of 1974 (C015-5) and not its spares: the AC-130U's radar, fire control and engines are not made at Bien Hoa, and nothing says where they came from after 1973; the same is true of the M855A1, the optics' batteries and the scopes of P004a and P004b (small-arms study Q-5); CP04 judges the wing flew 1974–75 partly by cannibalising grounded aircraft [X-CP04]

## Study: Air War (`studies/air-war.md`)
*Written ST04 · reflects the record after memo 015 · last folded — · tags: AIR.north_effect, AIR.north_defences, AIR.losses, VNAF.capability, STRIKE.responsiveness, TRAIL.capacity, TRAIL.tonnage_arriving, SANCT.laos, SANCT.cambodia, ARVN.effectiveness.fire_coordination, ARVN.self_sufficiency.fire_support, POP.civilian_harm, LOG.helicopter_hours*

### Summary
The air war in this record is history's air war with five new instruments in it, and its shape is set by one fact. American air power became far better at destroying what it could measure, and the enemy, within a season each time, stopped owning anything that could be measured. Three of the instruments were eyes and a hand that arrived on the war's first day: two U-2S Dragon Ladies and four RQ-4B Global Hawks to watch the enemy's roads, passes and dumps in any weather (P003a, P003b), and the re-engined B-52J replacing every B-52 one for one, with GPS-guided GBU-31 and GBU-38 bombs and Quickstrike mines and a coordinate cell at Tan Son Nhut to aim them (P005a–P005d). The fourth was an authority: from 2 March 1965 the northern campaign was run from Saigon on the theater's own list, with no zones around Hanoi or Haiphong and no pauses, and it opened with HAMMER FALL, a week that took the North's power, bulk fuel, great bridges, jet base and warning net (P013a, P013b; EV013-1). The fifth was a night gun. History's AC-47, AC-119 and AC-130 fleets never existed: from January 1964 sixty-four AC-130J Ghostriders of the US Air Force flew over the South's posts and the Trail, and from 1967 forty-eight AC-130U Spooky IIs of the Vietnamese Air Force took over the posts and kept them after the Americans left (P015a, P015b).

Each instrument changed something real, and the study weighs each at full weight. The interdiction debate became honest five years early: the radar counted the Trail's trucks from December 1965 and travelled to Washington beside every claim (EVR05-5, EV000-68). The measured siege became the enemy's worst battle: Con Thien lifted about three weeks early in 1967, Khe Sanh about two weeks early in 1968 with perhaps 3,500–4,000 PAVN dead to July against 2,469 acknowledged, and in 1972 the J's cells broke the penetration of An Loc on 12 May and the assault on Kontum short of the wire (EVCP02-3, EV000-41, EV000-76, EV000-77) [X-005]. The North's 1964 economy was wrecked in a week, three years before history's campaign reached it. Rolling Thunder lost about 810–880 aircraft rather than 922, and Linebacker II about six bombers rather than fifteen (POS013-3, EV000-82) [X-013] [X-005]. The night attack on a post, the Front's best tactic of the village war, lost a quarter to two-fifths of its effect in 1964–72 (F015-20), and in 1974 the Republic's own gunships held about 46 of 64 attacked canal posts in Chuong Thien (EV015-8) [X-015].

None of that reached the three things that decided the war, and the record says so as plainly as it records the gains. The flow south was taxed and never stopped: the study judges the Trail's capacity about 4–7 percent above history's from 1966, at low confidence, because a labour-rich enemy answered every precise cut with a redundant net (POS005-4). The bombing of the North, unrestricted from 1965, destroyed everything in the North that could be destroyed and the North's war in the South needed none of it (POS013-1). The main force under canopy was found no better than history found it (POS003-1, POS005-1). And almost none of the instruments belonged to the Republic. The cell, the bombers, the satellites' coordinates and the Ghostriders went home in 1972–73; the ARVN had learned to hold a besieged town and wait for bombs that no longer came, and at Phuoc Long in December 1974 the province chief asked for "the B-52 support provided for in the plan" (EV000-92).

The margin over history is therefore large inside the air war and small outside it. The one instrument the Republic owned changes the end of the war at the level of the posts, not of the divisions. At the end of 1975 the VNAF still exists, which history's did not after April, and it can lift, resupply, strike with unguided bombs and hold a post at night through cloud. It cannot fly over a PAVN division with its own air defence, and it cannot break a siege (POS015-4, G-12).

### Questions for the record
- **Q-1** · ERRATUM · EV000-68 (history/chapters/P4.md) states in its first paragraph, as part of the campaign's account, that "in Phase VII the AC-130E gunships were credited with 7,335 of 10,689 trucks claimed [H53]"; in this war no AC-130E existed (P015a), and DIRCP04-3 requires an event naming a replaced system to be altered or the sentence marked as history's. The sentence should read as history's figure, or be replaced by the Ghostriders' count of that phase.
- **Q-2** · CHECKPOINT · The headline ranges on *TRAIL.tonnage_arriving* (P6 −20% to +20%; P3 −17% to −5%; P2 −12% to −1%) and *ARVN.self_sufficiency.fire_support* (P2 and P3 −5 to +2; P6 +5 to +12) were written before R07 and are several times wider than A12b allows; the next checkpoint should narrow them around their midpoints with their confidence unchanged. The P6 tonnage range spans zero widely although its note gives a direction (a second dry season's offensive to carry).
- **Q-3** · CHECKPOINT · *ARVN.effectiveness* has no binding facet named in P5, P6 or the 1974 snapshot, so *fire_coordination* cannot be judged there, though the record holds evidence on it (EV000-76, EV000-77, EV000-91, F007-23, EV015-8); the next checkpoint should name the binding facet in those phases.
- **Q-4** · CHECKPOINT · *POP.civilian_harm* is judged by this study only to 1971; after 1970 the district chiefs who cleared fire beside the hamlets were the palace's choices (G-18), and the record holds no event on harm from the gunships in 1972–75. The gap stands open; a checkpoint should judge P5 and P6 or carry the gap.
- **Q-5** · CHECKPOINT · The record holds no total of AC-130J losses: it names Ghostrider 22 (March 1967, EVR05-5), two in 1970–71 (EV000-68) and the aircraft damaged at Tam Quan (EV015-1), against history's 31 gunships lost; nor a count of the VNAF at the end of 1975, nor the fate of the U-2S and the Global Hawks after 1973. A checkpoint should state the Ghostriders' losses for the war and what became of the record's reconnaissance aircraft.
- **Q-6** · CHECKPOINT · EVR05-5 places the "sixteen Ghostriders of the 17th Air Commando Squadron" at Ubon from December 1965, while memorandum 015's card puts the fourth squadron at "Nha Trang then Ubon" and EV015-6 has the 4th at Bien Hoa, the 14th at Nha Trang and the 16th at Da Nang; the squadron numbers and bases should be reconciled once (four squadrons of 16, which one went to Ubon and when).
- **Q-7** · STANDS · carried from ST01 Q-4 and the gap register (G-19): the record holds no account of Barrel Roll and the Plain of Jars after 1964, nor of the tactical air war in the South by sortie and its fall with the withdrawal; no variable measures the weight of American air power in the South.
- **Q-8** · RESOLVED · ST01 Q-2 asked whether Commando Hunt V's 8–10 percent net loss against history's 2 percent was effect or measurement; EV000-68 now attributes one to two points to the J and two to three to the Ghostriders, and the rest to the radar's honest count of the same effect, which this study takes.

## Study: US and ARVN small arms and individual weapons against the enemy's and against history (`studies/us-and-arvn-small-arms-and-individual-weapons-ag.md`)
*Written ST03 · reflects the record after memo 015 · last folded CP04 · tags: ARVN.effectiveness, RFPF.effectiveness, ARVN.self_sufficiency, ENEMY.engagement_control, FIX.capability, US.casualties, VC.main_force, VC.local_force, INTL.communist_aid*

### Summary
The Vietnam War was fought, at its bottom, by men carrying a rifle, a few grenades and whatever their squad could share: a machine gun, a grenade launcher, a rocket, a mine. This study first sets out what those men carried, on both sides and in every kind of force, and what each weapon could and could not do. It then follows the weapons through the six phases of this war as the record has it.

History's soldiers did not fight evenly armed. In January 1964 the Republic's regular infantry carried the American weapons of the Second World War and Korea: the eight-round M1 Garand, the light M1 and M2 carbines, the Browning Automatic Rifle (BAR) and the M1919 machine gun [M004] [M010]. Its Regional and Popular Forces carried the same weapons or older, and its CIDG strikers, police and hamlet militia carried what was left [S4] [S12]. Against them the Front was part-way through a rearmament with the Chinese and Soviet 7.62x39mm family: the AK-47 and its Chinese copy the Type 56, the SKS carbine, the RPD light machine gun, and the B40 rocket launcher [S1] [S3]. Historically the ARVN's infantry did not draw the M16, the M60 machine gun, the M79 grenade launcher and the M72 LAW until 1968, and the territorials until 1969 [S1]. The American soldier was better armed than either, but his M16 jammed in 1966–67 until a congressional inquiry forced the fixes of the M16A1 [S2].

This war changed three weapons and left the rest of the soldier's load alone. From 6 January 1964 every rifle and carbine in American and RVNAF hands, including those of the Regional and Popular Forces, was replaced by the M4A1 carbine with a red-dot sight. Every American and ARVN regular infantry squad also gained a belt-fed M249 light machine gun in place of its automatic rifle, and a marksman with a scoped M110A2 rifle (P004a, P004b, P004c) [M004]. The territorials kept the BAR as their automatic weapon (E04). The pistol, the grenade, the M60, the M79, the LAW, the Claymore, the shotgun, the mortar and the mine were history's, on both sides, throughout. So were the weapons of everyone the provision did not cover: the CIDG, the police, the Combat Youth and the People's Self-Defense Force, who inherited the Garands and carbines the army handed in. The enemy's weapons were history's too, with one addition: the 10,000–30,000 of the Republic's new carbines he had taken by the end of 1965 (F004-7) [X-004].

The record's verdict, stated in memorandum 004 and never reversed, is that the small arms changed how the fights the enemy accepted went, and never which fights he accepted (POS004-1). The margin over history was large for the territorials, who were not outgunned in the five years in which history's countryside was lost. It was large for the ARVN's regular infantry until history's army caught up in 1968, and modest for the Americans, whose own historical rifle was fixable and was fixed. The record puts the lives saved at about 1,000–2,500 American and 10,000–25,000 South Vietnamese over the war (F004-13) [X-004]. Those are judgments built on rates, not counts.

The enemy answered the rifle within a season. He stopped assaulting rearmed posts and attacked those the rearmament did not reach: the constables, the CIDG camps and the militia with the handed-down Garands. He moved his war from the rifle assault to the mortar, the sapper and the mine (F004-1, F004-2). From 1969 history's army carried the same class of rifle, and the remaining margin was the squad gun, the marksman and practice (POS004-2). In 1974 the margin became a cost, when an army built around the belt-fed gun met the ammunition ration (F004-15). The end state, rung (b), a reprieve of about a year, was decided far above the squad.

### Questions for the record
- **Q-1** · RESOLVED · erratum E04 and revision R04 corrected EV006-2 and EV007-3 to carbines and BARs; the Regional Forces never drew the M249.
- **Q-2** · RESOLVED · CP04 made EV000-56 HIST-ALT: the programme bought no new rifle in this war, and its small-arms money replaced worn carbines and sights, bought M855A1 for the territorial expansion and added M60s.
- **Q-3** · RESOLVED · CP04 reversed POS004-3 (REVCP04-1): the Hue hoard was destroyed in place on 17 April 1975, what the Highlands and Quang Ngai held went with them in April, and the stocks of III and IV Corps remain the Republic's.
- **Q-4** · STANDS · carried to the gap register under G-10: the record holds no ledger of the Republic's small arms lost after 1966, or of how long the Front kept the captured carbines once the North's 7.62x39mm reached the village level.
- **Q-5** · STANDS · carried to the gap register as G-20: whether Bien Hoa loaded the M855A1 or a simpler ball round, and whether the CompM5's batteries and the TANGO6T scopes were kept up after 1973, is untraced.
- **Q-6** · ERRATUM · the police's weapons disagree across the record. Memorandum 002, Part 1, P002a's weapons field, stipulated [U], arms each village constable with the M4 carbine and a Remington 870-class pump shotgun, puts an M60 in every village post, and gives the Police Field Force the M16A1 from the start. Memorandum 004 (P004a negative specification, F004-1 and its interaction with P002a) says the rearmament "does not arm the National Police, the Police Field Force" and that the constables "keep their carbines". The chapters follow memorandum 004: EV002-2 gives the posts "ten constables carrying the carbines of 1950", and EV004-1 sends a third of the handed-in weapons to the police. Memorandum 006 Part 1 arms the PRUs with "what the Police Field Force carries in this war: M1 and M2 carbines, the M1918A2 automatic rifle and M79 grenade launchers". One account must give way, and because P002a's weapons were stipulated by the user, the user's ruling decides which. If memorandum 002 stands, the constables' deaths of 1964–65 and the Front's choice of police posts as soft targets (F004-1) need re-reading.
- **Q-7** · CHECKPOINT · the reach of P004a beyond the line rifle is unrecorded. Memorandum 004 replaces "every M16, M1 Garand, M1 and M2 carbine and M14", which on its words includes the M21 sniper rifle, a scoped M14, yet memorandum 004 itself treats the M21 and the M40 as history's snipers still serving. It also notes that the M203 will not mount on the URG-I rail without an adaptor and leaves open whether grenadiers kept a separate M16A1 or the depots made an interface. A checkpoint should say what history's snipers and, from 1969, history's grenadiers carried in this war.
- **Q-8** · RESOLVED · ST02's own text said the Long Huu post's BARs "had been replaced by carbines with 30-round magazines", which EV004-1 ("the outposts kept the Browning as their automatic rifle") and erratum E04 contradict; this re-run tells the night with the platoon's BAR.

Also checked and found consistent: the American historical baseline (the M14, the M16's 1966–67 failures, the 1967 subcommittee and the M16A1; EVCP02-3 against [S2]); the ARVN's historical rearmament dates (EV000-51 and memorandum 004 against [S1]); the squad-gun counts (one per ARVN squad, two per Army squad, three per Marine squad, against P004c); the marksman ranges in the events (300–800 m) against P004b's practical range; and the weapons the record gives the enemy in each event against [S3] and [S4].

### Since this study
